3.text: The Moon has a lasso with which he catches such people, and hauls them

4.text: upward. He thus captured a boy or a girl, or both, according to different

5.text: versions of the story. They may now be seen on the moon, by the side of

6.text: the Moon-Man. Other informants said that the Moon carried away the boy

7.text: because he was ill-treated by his step-mother. Because the Moon has a

8.text: lasso, he accepts offerings of small pieces of thong. The Moon is also said

9.text: to have attempted to ravish a girl, and to have been prevented by her

10.text: pinioning his arms to his sides until he had to plead to be released.

11.text: In one tale a shaman named Attɪˊg̣ɪtkɪ went with his cousin to the sea.

12.text: On the open sea they saw a small old man sitting on the water with legs

13.text: crossed, and covering the entrance to the world under water. By promising

14.text: to give him, on their return home, an old blind she-dog, gray with age, they

15.text: were permitted to enter. Descending to the world under water, they walked

16.text: along and found still another world supported in the air on the end of a

17.text: long needle. They turned into mosquitoes, flew upward, and slipped through

18.text: the needle’s eye into that world. Then they became men again.

19.text: The owner of that world is the Earth (Nuˊtenut). He sits in a large

20.text: iron house surrounded by Sun, Moon, Sky, Sea, Dawn, Darkness, and

21.text: World, who are suitors for his beautiful daughter. Their hands are covered

22.text: with scars, because at each meal, when the tray with the meat is brought

23.text: in, the master strikes with a long knife at every hand that reaches out for

24.text: the food. The guests, however, being powerful shamans, immediately heal

25.text: their wounds by breathing on them. Attɪˊg̣ɪtkɪ sits down by himself, puts

26.text: his cap on his lap, and draws in his breath. Plenty of meat jumps over

27.text: into the cap, and Nuˊtenut has no occasion to interfere.

28.text: After the meal the suitors are sent to fetch fuel. A large tree-trunk

29.text: stands up in the middle of the sea. As soon as a suitor climbs it and

30.text: begins to cut its branches with an axe, the “spirit” that lives in the tree-

31.text: trunk shakes it, and the wood-cutter falls down and is drowned. The suitors,

32.text: being shamans, rise again, and come back to the shore. Attɪˊg̣ɪtkɪ and his

33.text: cousin bring a quantity of food and drop it on the tree-trunk. While the

34.text: “spirit” is busy eating the food, they succeed in cutting off a piece of wood

35.text: as large as a house. After a while a shamanistic contest begins in the

36.text: sleeping-room. The lights are extinguished. Sun brings his luminary, and

37.text: scorches the people. Sea brings the flood, and drowns everything. Moon

38.text: brings the “shutting rocks,” and crushes the competitors. Dawn brings two

39.text: polar bears, which eat everybody. Darkness brings two black bears, which do

40.text: the same. Sky makes its upper hard crust fall down and crush the people.

41.text: Worlds brings a blizzard, and freezes them. After each performance, all the

42.text: rival shamans come to life again. The two men remain unhurt, because
